summary.name: Global Positioning System (GPS)
summary.one_liner: GPS is the US-owned satellite navigation system that gives a receiver anywhere on or near Earth its location and time, without the receiver transmitting any data.
use_cases: Finding your location with a GPS receiver or smartphone
Getting accurate time from satellite signals
Surveying and engineering positioning with high-precision receivers
Understanding GPS history and how it was developed
summary.what_it_does: The page describes GPS as a satellite-based navigation system owned by the US Space Force and operated by Mission Delta 31, providing geolocation and time to receivers worldwide where signal quality permits. Receivers work independently of phone or internet reception, though those can improve results. The page covers the system's history from its 1973 start and 1978 first launch, through the removal of Selective Availability in 2000, to modernization efforts such as GPS Block III and L5 signals. It also gives accuracy figures: about 5 m for civilian use after Selective Availability ended, around 30 cm for L5-capable receivers, and about 2 cm or better for surveying equipment. The principles section explains that position is calculated from signal travel time measured against synchronized atomic clocks on the satellites.
notable: Operated by the US Space Force (Mission Delta 31) and freely accessible to anyone with a GPS receiver
Constellation of 24 nominal satellites in 6 medium-earth-orbit planes, with 31 operational as of the page
Selective Availability, the deliberate civilian accuracy degradation, was disabled on May 1, 2000
Accuracy ranges from about 5 m for standard civilian receivers to sub-centimeter for long-term surveying
caveats: OCX, the Next Generation Operational Control System, was canceled in April 2026 according to the page
Accuracy depends on receiver and antenna quality and atmospheric conditions; signal quality limits where it works
Full availability of 24 L5 satellites is expected only in 2027, per the page
